args.text:
Committee Policy Actions
So the Committee's got its dual-mandate goals to look after, and to back them every last member agreed to whack the target range for the federal funds rate up by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 per cent. They stuck with the FOMC's policy of keeping ample reserves in the banking system while they were at it. Members noted the unemployment rate had barely budged, and solid growth in economic activity had kept chugging along, with domestic spending holding up like a good stump. Inflation, though, was still running hot against the Committee's 2 per cent goal, and that's the bit that's got their goat. The Committee made it plain it's still dead set on its dual-mandate goals, putting it in black and white in the postmeeting statement that it "will deliver price stability." No ifs or buts. Members agreed the policy action they'd taken would help get inflation back to the Committee's 2 per cent goal sooner rather than later.

Once they'd talked it all through, the Committee voted to direct the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, till it hears otherwise, to carry out transactions in the System Open Market Account in line with the following domestic policy directive, for release at 2:00 p.m. Here it is, word for word:

"Effective September 17, 2026, the Federal Open Market Committee directs the Desk to:

Undertake open market operations as necessary to maintain the federal funds rate in a target range of 3-3/4 to 4 percent.

Conduct standing overnight repurchase agreement operations at a rate of 4.0 percent.

Conduct standing overnight reverse repurchase agreement operations at an offering rate of 3.75 percent and with a per-counterparty limit of $160 billion per day.

When appropriate, increase the System Open Market Account holdings of securities through purchases of Treasury bills and, if needed, other Treasury securities with remaining maturities of 3 years or less to maintain an ample level of reserves.

Roll over at auction all principal payments from the Federal Reserve's holdings of Treasury securities. Reinvest all principal payments from the Federal Reserve's holdings of agency securities into Treasury bills."

The same vote took in sign-off on the statement below as well, for release at 2:00 p.m. Word for word again:

"The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 12–0 vote:

The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."

Voting for this action: Kevin Warsh, John C. Williams, Michael S. Barr, Michelle W. Bowman, Lisa D. Cook, Beth M. Hammack, Philip N. Jefferson, Neel Kashkari, Lorie K. Logan, Anna Paulson, Jerome H. Powell, and Christopher J. Waller.

Voting against this action: None. Not a single one.

Then, going along with the Committee's decision to lift the target range for the federal funds rate to 3-3/4 to 4 per cent, the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System voted unanimously to bump up the interest rate paid on reserve balances to 3.90 per cent, effective September 17, 2026. And the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System voted unanimously to give a 1/4 percentage point increase the nod too, taking the primary credit rate to 4.0 per cent, effective September 17, 2026.2

Everyone agreed the Committee's next get-together would be held on Tuesday–Wednesday, October 27–28, 2026. They called it a day at 10:15 a.m. on September 16, 2026.

Notation Vote
By notation vote wrapped up on August 18, 2026, the Committee unanimously signed off on the minutes of the Committee meeting held on July 28–29, 2026.
